71.event_title: Jim Redmond helps his injured son Derek finish the Olympic 400 metres
71.event: In the 400 metres semi-final at the Barcelona Olympics, the British runner Derek Redmond tore his hamstring on the back straight and began hobbling towards the finish alone. His father, Jim Redmond, came down from the stands, got past the stewards, put his arm around his son and helped him along the track. Just before the line his father let go, and Derek finished the race as a crowd of about 65,000 stood to applaud.
71.explanation: The father's love could not be held back by rules, officials or the setting of an Olympic stadium; it showed itself openly and at once when his son was suffering.
71.tie_back: The kural asks whether any bolt can lock love in, and a father pushing past security to hold his weeping son shows love breaking out the moment a loved one is in pain.
71._accuracy_note: A very close dramatisation of love made visible by a loved one's suffering, though the kural's specific image is a tear rather than an action.

72.event_title: Maximilian Kolbe offers his life for a fellow prisoner at Auschwitz
72.event: After a prisoner escaped from Auschwitz in July 1941, ten men were selected to be starved to death in reprisal. When one of them, Franciszek Gajowniczek, pleaded for his wife and children, the Polish Franciscan priest Maximilian Kolbe stepped forward and asked to take his place, and the SS accepted. Kolbe died in the cellar of Block 11 on 14 August 1941; Gajowniczek survived the war, and Kolbe was canonised in 1982.
72.explanation: Kolbe gave up his own body and life for a stranger, the furthest extent to which a person can give themselves to another.
72.tie_back: The kural says the loving regard even their own bones as belonging to others, and Kolbe literally gave his body in exchange for another man's life.
72._accuracy_note: Almost a literal enactment of giving even one's bones to others, documented by the Auschwitz Memorial and the survivor himself.

73.event_title: Viktor Frankl writes Man's Search for Meaning
73.event: The Viennese psychiatrist Viktor Frankl was held in four Nazi camps, including Auschwitz, between 1942 and 1945, while his wife, parents and brother died. After liberation he dictated, within nine days, the book later published in English as Man's Search for Meaning. In it he describes a winter march during which he held on to the image of his wife and concluded that love reaches far beyond the physical person of the beloved and finds its deepest meaning in the beloved's inner self.
73.explanation: Frankl's account, written from the extremity of the camps, argues that the meaning of a human life is found in love, even when the body is reduced to bare survival.
73.tie_back: The kural claims that the soul's union with the body exists for the sake of love, and Frankl found that, stripped of everything else, love was what gave his embodied life its point.
73._accuracy_note: Frankl's documented conclusion closely matches the kural's teleological reading, but it is a reflection recorded in a book rather than a single public event.

74.event_title: Jesse Owens and Luz Long become friends at the Berlin Olympics
74.event: At the 1936 Berlin Olympics the American Jesse Owens won the long jump gold medal and the German Luz Long took silver. Owens later wrote that what he remembered most was the friendship he struck up with Long, and the two corresponded by letter until the war broke out in 1939. Long was killed in the Second World War in 1943, and after the war Owens kept up the friendship through correspondence with Long's son.
74.explanation: A warm regard between two rivals, formed in the most politically charged Games of the century, grew into a friendship that outlasted a war and a death.
74.tie_back: The kural traces a lineage from love to warm eagerness to friendship, an unsought excellence, and the Owens and Long friendship arose unlooked-for out of goodwill between competitors.
74._accuracy_note: A well-documented friendship that came unsought out of goodwill, though the sources do not trace the inner steps from affection to friendship the kural describes; the disputed advice story is deliberately left out.

75.event_title: Elizabeth Barrett and Robert Browning marry and settle in Florence
75.event: The poets Elizabeth Barrett and Robert Browning, whose courtship began with letters in 1845, married secretly at St Marylebone Parish Church in London in September 1846 and a week later left for Italy, because her father would not allow any of his children to marry. They made their home at Casa Guidi in Florence for fourteen years, where her health improved markedly and their son Pen was born in 1849. Both continued to write and became among the most celebrated poets of their age until her death in 1861.
75.explanation: The Brownings' marriage is one of the best-documented examples of a life built around love that also brought health, creativity and lasting public distinction.
75.tie_back: The kural says the distinction of those who live happily in this world is the fruit of a life settled in love, and the Brownings' settled married life in Florence was the setting for their happiest and most admired years.
75._accuracy_note: A good documented example of happiness and renown flowing from a loving life, though their fame as poets began before the marriage.

76.event_title: Desmond Doss rescues wounded comrades on Okinawa
76.event: Desmond Doss, a Seventh-day Adventist and conscientious objector, served as an unarmed US Army medic with the 77th Infantry Division because he refused to carry a rifle. During the Battle of Okinawa he went repeatedly into exposed ground under fire and is credited with bringing about 75 wounded men to safety, and he was himself wounded several times. On 12 October 1945 President Truman presented him with the Medal of Honor, the first awarded to a conscientious objector.
76.explanation: Doss's extraordinary battlefield courage came not from hostility but from devotion to the men around him, showing that love can drive the hardest physical bravery.
76.tie_back: The kural rebukes those who think love supports only gentle virtue, and Doss showed love powering valour in the midst of war.
76._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of love fuelling courage in war, though Doss's bravery was protective rather than martial in the sense of fighting.

77.event_title: Belgium takes the Congo Free State from King Leopold II
77.place: Congo Free State (now Democratic Republic of the Congo) and Brussels, Belgium
77.event: From 1885 King Leopold II ruled the Congo Free State as his personal possession, forcing its people to gather rubber and ivory for export by brutal methods. Reports such as Roger Casement's investigation for the British government and campaigns by E. D. Morel, missionaries and writers including Mark Twain produced an international outcry. In 1908 the Belgian parliament annexed the territory, ending the king's personal rule over it.
77.explanation: A regime run purely for profit, with no regard for the people it ruled, was brought down by the moral outrage it provoked across the world.
77.tie_back: The kural says righteousness scorches the loveless as the sun scorches a boneless worm, and Leopold's pitiless rule could not withstand the moral exposure turned on it.
77._accuracy_note: A reasonable illustration of a cruel enterprise undone by moral pressure, though Leopold was paid for the colony and abuses did not end at once.

78.event_title: The world learns of Romania's state orphanages
78.event: After the fall of the Ceausescu government at the end of 1989, the outside world learned of large state institutions in which abandoned children were raised with severe psychosocial deprivation; one Bucharest institution held about 850 children under three in 1989. From 2000 the Bucharest Early Intervention Project compared institutionalised children with those placed in foster families. It found that children who stayed in institutions scored far below the others in development, and that foster care, especially when begun early, improved cognitive and emotional outcomes.
78.explanation: The Romanian findings showed that bodily care without love and attention produces only the outward form of a growing child, not a flourishing one.
78.tie_back: The kural compares a loveless life to a dead tree putting out shoots in the desert, an appearance of life with nothing behind it, and the orphanage children's stunted development proved how much love is needed for real growth.
78._accuracy_note: Strong scientific evidence that life without affection is a diminished semblance of life, though it concerns children deprived of love rather than people who withhold it.

79.event_title: Harry Harlow presents The Nature of Love
79.event: In his 1958 presidential address to the American Psychological Association, titled The Nature of Love, the psychologist Harry Harlow reported experiments in which infant rhesus monkeys were given a bare wire surrogate mother and a cloth-covered one. The infants went to the wire figure only to feed, if it held the bottle, and spent their time clinging to the soft cloth figure, especially when frightened. The work showed that comfort and contact, not feeding alone, were the basis of attachment.
79.explanation: Harlow's experiments demonstrated that meeting a creature's bodily needs is not enough; an inner bond of comfort is what makes development possible.
79.tie_back: The kural asks what use the outer limbs are without love, the body's inner organ, and Harlow showed that the food-giving apparatus was nearly worthless to the infants without the comfort of contact.
79._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the experiment shows the primacy of love-like comfort over bodily provision, but the kural is about a person lacking love, not an infant deprived of it, and the research is now viewed as ethically troubling.

80.event_title: Baba Amte founds Anandwan for people with leprosy
80.event: Murlidhar Devidas Amte, known as Baba Amte, gave up a prosperous legal career to serve people with leprosy, who were widely shunned. In 1951, with his family, six leprosy patients and a lame cow, he settled on a stretch of stony wasteland in Chandrapur district and built Anandwan, the Forest of Joy, a self-supporting community run by and for people with the disease. He received the Ramon Magsaysay Award in 1985 and shared the Templeton Prize in 1990.
80.explanation: Amte's whole life was organised around love for people others rejected, and it turned barren land into a living community.
80.tie_back: The kural says a body that moves along the path of love is truly alive, and Amte's life, spent in the service of the shunned, is a vivid example of that path.
80._accuracy_note: A reasonable illustration of a life animated by love, though the kural's sharper point concerns the deadness of the loveless, which this event shows only by contrast.
